note: Worked examples: one Normal and one Anomalous group per dataset, the same for every participant. These groups are excluded from every task, group count, member count, time total and accuracy figure.

examples.title: BGL worked example — Normal
examples.summary: Template <*> L3 <*> error(s) (dcr <*> detected and corrected — component KERNEL, level INFO.
examples.sample: … RAS KERNEL INFO 1 L3 EDRAM error(s) (dcr 0x0157) detected and corrected
steps: Read the header: component KERNEL, severity INFO. Rule B-N01 is the first BGL rule: the severity is not FATAL or FAILURE.
Open the Fields tab: field 1 is a count, field 2 is EDRAM or directory, field 3 is a register address. No value can turn an INFO line into an alert.
Click a few messages to read their raw lines, and open the context of one line. Every line shows RAS KERNEL INFO.
examples.explanation: B-N01 decides for every line of the group: the severity is INFO. The word “error” in the message does not matter; only FATAL and FAILURE lines can be alerts, and only when an alert rule matches. Label for the group: Normal.

examples.title: BGL worked example — Anomalous
examples.summary: Template Lustre mount FAILED : <*> : block_id : location — component KERNEL, level FATAL.
examples.sample: … RAS KERNEL FATAL Lustre mount FAILED : bglio17 : block_id : location
steps: Read the header: component KERNEL, severity FATAL. B-N01 does not apply: FATAL lines can be alerts, so go through B-A01 … B-A11.
B-A04 needs the phrase Lustre mount FAILED. The phrase lies in the fixed text of the template, so it matches every line of the group.
Open the Fields tab: field 1 is the I/O node (bglio16, bglio17, …). The node is a detail of the failure; it does not change the rule.
examples.explanation: B-A04 matches every line of the group: Lustre mount FAILED is part of the template's fixed text. One matching line is already enough for the group. Label for the group: Anomalous.

examples.title: Thunderbird worked example — Normal
examples.sample: acpid: acpid startup succeeded  /  acpid: acpid shutdown succeeded
steps: Go through T-A01 … T-A10: no alert phrase appears in the template, and field 2 only takes the values startup / shutdown, which cannot complete any alert phrase.
Click each of the two messages to read their raw lines.
Open the context of a line: it sits in a run of service start / stop records written while a node boots or shuts down. Context does not change the label; it only confirms what you read.
examples.explanation: No rule T-A01 … T-A10 applies to any line of the group, so T-N01 decides. Label for the group: Normal.

examples.title: Thunderbird worked example — Anomalous
examples.summary: Template [KERNEL_IB][tsIbTavorMadProcess][…/tavor_mad.c:<*>]InfiniHost0: EVAPI_process_local_mad failed, return code = -<*> (Fatal error (Local Catastrophic Error)) — service kernel.
examples.sample: kernel: [KERNEL_IB][tsIbTavorMadProcess][/mnt_projects/…/tavor_mad.c:152]InfiniHost0: EVAPI_process_local_mad failed, return code = -254 (Fatal error (Local Catastrophic Error))
steps: T-A01 needs both [KERNEL_IB] and Local Catastrophic Error. Both lie in the fixed text of the template, so every line of the group matches.
Open the Fields tab: the values are a software version, a build directory, a source line and a return code. They do not affect the rule.
Click the message and open the context of one line. Context does not change the label; it only shows the surrounding records.
examples.explanation: T-A01 matches every line of the group. Label for the group: Anomalous. Not every [KERNEL_IB] message is an alert: Local Catastrophic Error must be in the line as well.

examples.title: HDFS worked example — Normal
examples.summary: Count vector: allocate T22×1; write three replicas T5, T9, T11, T26 ×3 each; read T3×1 and T4 (Got exception while serving) ×2; verify T2×3; file deletion T23, T21 ×3 each.
steps: H-A01: none of the failure events T7, T8, T10, T12, T13, T14, T17, T20, T24, T27, T28, T29, T31, T32 is in the count vector.
H-A02: the write is complete (T22 ≥ 1, T5 ≥ 3, T9 ≥ 3, T11 ≥ 3, T26 ≥ 3). H-A03: there is no T25. H-U01: no T1, T15, T19. H-N02: no T25.
Open the full log of 2–3 blocks and compare two of them: their event orders differ, but every one is write 3 replicas → read and verify → delete 3 replicas. T4 belongs to the read phase.
examples.explanation: No rule above H-N01 applies, so H-N01 decides. All blocks of the group share the count vector, so the group gets one label: Normal. The order of events does not matter.

examples.title: HDFS worked example — Anomalous
examples.summary: Count vector: allocate T22×1; write three replicas T5, T9, T11 ×3 each, T26×4; file deletion T23, T21 ×3 each; T28 (addStoredBlock request received … But it does not belong to any file) ×1.
examples.sample: BLOCK* NameSystem.addStoredBlock: addStoredBlock request received for blk_… on 10.251.106.10:50010 size 67108864 But it does not belong to any file.
steps: H-A01: the count vector contains T28, one of the failure events. No other rule needs to be checked.
Open a block's log and find the T28 line: after the file was deleted (T23, T21), a data node reported the block again and the name node answered that the block does not belong to any file.
The rest of the trace is a complete write. One failure event is enough to make the block anomalous.
examples.explanation: H-A01 decides: T28 is in the count vector (Xu et al., Table 7, type 5: received block that does not belong to any file). All blocks of the group share the count vector, so the group gets one label: Anomalous.
